Housing assistance / 4–6 min

You have
the voucher.
Can you find
a home?

Rental assistance is an important beginning. Follow the distance between approval and a signed lease.

By Megan Quigley · A synthesis of published research

Follow the story ↓

From approval to a front-door key

01 Benefit02 Search03 Barriers04 Leases05 Support06 Delivery

01 / Benefit

Approved

A voucher can change what a household can afford. Through the Housing Choice Voucher program, a local housing agency uses federal funding to pay part of the rent directly to a landlord. The household pays its share.

This story begins when the voucher is issued. A home still has to be found. Approval is a milestone worth recognizing, and it is the point where a different kind of work begins.

What would you count as success here: assistance issued, or a household able to use it?

HUD: how housing vouchers work ↗

02 / Search

Now find somewhere to use it

A promising rental listing is the start of an approval process. The renter and landlord complete tenancy paperwork. The housing agency checks the home’s condition and whether the proposed rent is reasonable. The lease and assistance arrangements must be completed.

These steps involve three parties: the household, the landlord, and the housing agency. Health and safety checks serve a purpose. The practical question is whether the process helps people reach a suitable home in time.

A voucher also has a search deadline. HUD advises recipients who need more time to contact their housing agency about an extension. The one-year window used later in this story is a research measure; it is not a promise that every household gets a year to search.

HUD: searching, tenancy approval, and extensions ↗

03 / Barriers

The doors that stay closed

One obstacle appears before inspection or a signed lease: whether a landlord will accept the voucher.

A HUD-sponsored study published in 2018 tested landlord acceptance in five locations. Reported voucher-denial rates were 78% in Fort Worth, 76% in Los Angeles, 67% in Philadelphia, 31% in Newark, and 15% in Washington, DC.

Compare the five places. The same kind of rental assistance encountered very different levels of rejection. These are historical study results, not a description of every landlord or today’s local rules.

The comparison identifies one barrier. It does not tell us why every voucher search fails, and it cannot be subtracted from the separate lease-up figures that follow.

Urban Institute: five-site landlord acceptance study, published 2018 ↗

04 / Leases

From voucher to lease

Now widen the view from landlord responses to completed searches.

A HUD-funded analysis published in 2025 estimated that 57.3% of searches by new voucher recipients led to a lease within one year in 2022. In 2020, the figure was 65.7%.

Imagine 100 searches: roughly 57 end with a lease within that window. The remaining searches did not record that outcome. This is a measure of whether issued assistance became usable housing support, not a count of all households needing help.

The analysis included 1,232 housing agencies meeting data-quality standards. Smaller and rural agencies were underrepresented. These records reveal an outcome gap; they do not supply a complete explanation for it.

Furman Center: sample and one-year success rates, pages 8–10 ↗

05 / Support

Help with the search

What happens when assistance includes help navigating the search itself?

In Seattle and King County, a randomized trial offered a bundle of support: information about neighborhoods, customized search assistance, connections to landlords, and short-term financial help. The share of families moving to neighborhoods with high upward mobility rose from 15% in the control group to 53% in the treatment group.

This is a different question from whether a family found any home. The result concerns where families moved. It supports a narrower conclusion: in this setting, practical support expanded access to particular neighborhoods.

The trial tested a package of help. A simple animation should not suggest that any one ingredient produced the entire effect.

Opportunity Insights: Creating Moves to Opportunity randomized trial ↗

06 / Delivery

What counts as delivery?

Return to the voucher. The paper represents a commitment of public resources. The key represents a household able to use that commitment.

The evidence asks us to pay attention to the space between them. A useful evaluation should follow what happens after approval: the search, the obstacles, and the outcome. It should also ask which forms of support change what people can do.

Which part of the journey could a better public service make easier?

What this story can tell us

This story begins after a voucher is issued. The 2022 outcome is a one-year lease-up estimate at agencies passing data-quality checks. The landlord study and neighborhood trial have different populations and outcomes. None measures access among everyone eligible for housing assistance.

Illustrations explain a process. They do not depict an interviewed person. Recommendations and editorial questions are labeled separately from measured results.
